title: Counting to 100 in Grade 1: Hundred Chart, Skip Counting & Counting Back + Free Quiz
meta_title: Counting to 100 for Grade 1 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Help your Grade 1 child count to 100 with the hundred chart, skip counting by 2s, 5s and 10s, and a free 8-question quiz plus printable practice.
excerpt: Almost every six-year-old can rattle off one to twenty. The wall goes up at the decade bridges — 29 to 30, 39 to 40. Here is how to get a Grade 1 child counting to 100 with real understanding, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Listen to a Grade 1 child counting out loud and you can almost hear where the road ends. They sail through one to twenty-nine, confident and quick — and then, at the edge of the next ten, comes the stumble: ‘twenty-nine… twenty-ten? twenty-eleven?’ Counting to 100 in Grade 1 is rarely blocked by the big numbers themselves. It is blocked by a handful of tricky corners called the decade bridges, and once a child crosses those cleanly, the rest of the hundred falls into place.

I have watched dozens of six-year-olds hit exactly this wall. The fix is not more chanting from one. It is a good tool, a bit of counting backwards, and skip counting — the three things this post is about.

The decade bridges are where counting really breaks

English number names hide a nasty little trap. From 21 to 29 the pattern is steady: twenty-one, twenty-two, and so on. But the jump from 29 to 30 asks the child to do two things at once — drop back to ‘one’ in the units and switch the ten-word from twenty to thirty. That double switch is genuinely hard, and it repeats at every 39 to 40, 49 to 50, right up the chart.

So drill the bridges directly. Do not always start at one. Start at 27 and ask the child to count to 33. Start at 58 and go to 62. When you isolate the crossing — ‘what comes right after 39?’ — you are practising the exact spot that fails, instead of burning energy on the easy stretches in between.

The hundred chart is the tool worth owning

If you buy or print one thing for Grade 1 number work, make it a hundred chart: a 10 × 10 grid with 1 in the top-left and 100 in the bottom-right. It turns counting from a memory task into a spatial one, and that changes everything.

On the chart, patterns become visible. Move one square right and the number goes up by one. Move one square down and it jumps by ten — 24 sits directly above 34, which sits above 44. Children who cannot yet explain place value can still see that every number in a column ends in the same digit. That picture does more quiet teaching than any worksheet of loose sums.

Three quick games on the chart

  • Cover and guess: hide one number with a coin and ask which is missing. The child uses the neighbours to work it out.
  • Race the rows: point to 47 and ask for the number just below (57) and just above (37). This builds the ‘add ten, take ten’ instinct.
  • Colour the count: shade every number you land on while skip counting — the staircases and stripes that appear are the whole point.

Counting backwards is not optional

Most parents drill forwards and forget the other direction entirely. That is a mistake. A child who can count back from 20 — twenty, nineteen, eighteen — has understood that numbers sit in a fixed order you can travel both ways, and that idea is the seed of subtraction. It is also harder than counting up, so it exposes gaps a forward count hides.

Keep it playful. Count down the last ten seconds before the school bus, or count backwards while walking down a flight of stairs, one number per step. Ten focused seconds a day is plenty.

Skip counting by 2s, 5s and 10s

Skip counting is counting in equal jumps instead of ones. Start with tens, because it is the easiest and the most useful: 10, 20, 30, 40. Then fives: 5, 10, 15, 20 — and here the hundred chart earns its keep, because the fives fall in two tidy columns you can point to. Twos come last: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.

Anchor each one to something real. Tens are rupee coins or bundles of ten. Fives are the fingers on one hand, then two hands. Twos are pairs of shoes lined up at the door. In my experience, the child who counts real objects in groups holds the pattern far longer than the child who only chants it.

Why skip counting quietly seeds multiplication

Here is the part most people miss. When a child counts 5, 10, 15, 20 and knows they made four jumps of five, they have just worked out 4 × 5 without anyone saying the word multiplication. Skip counting is multiplication wearing a disguise. Every group of fives your child counts in Grade 1 is a table they will not have to cram in Grade 2. That is the strongest reason to take it seriously now, well before the tables arrive.

How the counting skills fit together

Skip counting by 10sThe easiest big-number pattern10, 20, 30… to 100
Skip counting by 5s and 2sEarly groups (seeds multiplication)5, 10, 15, 20…

A realistic week

You do not need a lesson plan. Two minutes of bridge-crossing on the way to school, one hundred-chart game after dinner, a backward count on the stairs, and one skip-counting chant while setting the table. Spread across the day like that, counting stops feeling like homework and starts feeling like a habit. One honest caveat: resist testing to 100 too early. A child who counts confidently to 50 with understanding is in far better shape than one who has parroted to 100 but freezes at every decade bridge.

quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on the next number, the decade bridges, counting back and skip counting. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 1 counting and number sequences to 100

questions.explanation: This is a decade bridge. After 29 the units reset to zero and the ten-word changes, so 29 is followed by 30.
Counting by fives means adding five each jump. After 15 comes 20.
Counting back means going down by one. After 13 comes 12.
Counting by twos means adding two each jump. After 8 comes 10.
The number just before 40 is 39. This is the tricky decade bridge, counted the backward way.
Counting by tens adds ten each jump. After 50 comes 60.
Counting up by ones, the number between 48 and 50 is 49.

questions.q: Counting by fives 5, 10, 15, 20, how many jumps of five did you make?
questions.explanation: The jumps are 5, 10, 15, 20 — four jumps of five. That is the same as 4 × 5, which is why skip counting is early multiplication.

faq.q: By when should a Grade 1 child count to 100?
faq.a: Most children reach a reliable count to 100 across Grade 1, usually by the second half of the year. Counting confidently to 50 with understanding first, including the decade bridges, matters more than rushing to 100.

faq.q: What is a hundred chart and why does it help?
faq.a: It is a 10 by 10 grid of the numbers 1 to 100. It turns counting into a visual pattern — move right to add one, move down to add ten — so children can see the structure instead of memorising a long list.

faq.q: My child says twenty-ten instead of thirty. How do I fix it?
faq.a: That is the classic decade-bridge slip. Practise just the crossings: start counting from 27 up to 33, or ask directly what comes after 39. Drilling the exact tricky spot works far better than restarting from one every time.

faq.q: Is skip counting really needed this early?
faq.a: Yes. Counting in 10s, 5s and 2s is early multiplication in disguise — four jumps of five is 4 times 5. Children who skip count fluently in Grade 1 find the times tables in Grade 2 far less of a shock.
